prize_parts.citation: for empirical and conceptual analyses of how technology and trade shape labour demand, wage inequality and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: The B009 achievement is a connected body of work that explains how technological change and import competition alter labour demand, wage structure and the costs of adjustment. Katz and co-authors established the skill-premium and wage-structure facts. Autor and co-authors added the task-based account of job polarisation. Autor, Dorn and Hanson then documented the local labour-market effects of import competition with transparent quasi-experimental designs. The core findings have been replicated and challenged for more than a decade and have largely held. The work has also changed policy discussion of displacement and adjustment assistance. Under common criteria (the importance of what was learned, the credibility of identification, maturity and attribution), I still find this the strongest candidate on the list. The main reason is that the evidence is the kind that lets us say what was identified, not only that an effect exists. B014 is close behind: Melitz and Helpman gave trade a firm-level foundation, and trade has not been recognised since 2008. B014 has more diffuse priority issues, however, and the welfare-gain magnitudes depend on modelling assumptions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. A three-name limit leaves out David Dorn, a full co-author of the central China-shock papers. It also splits credit between two strands, technology and trade, which some members may regard as separate achievements. The task framework has co-originators who are not on the ballot (Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu and Restrepo on the theory side). External validity and persistence of the shift-share trade-shock estimates remain debated. The committee could reasonably prefer a narrower prize anchored in the trade-shock evidence alone.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B009 first but proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn. His view is that the credible, replicated China-shock evidence is the core of the achievement, and that Katz's skill-premium work is a parallel contribution whose credit boundary is contestable.
responses.response: I take Dorn's claim seriously. If the citation were confined to the trade-shock evidence, Autor, Dorn and Hanson would be the cleaner trio, and I would support it. I keep Katz because my proposed citation covers the technology and wage-structure strand and the trade strand together, and Katz is the long-run anchor of the first. Autor is the only person who spans both. The choice therefore depends on how broadly the committee defines the discovery. I do not think the number of colleagues who proposed one trio or the other settles that question. The relevant test is whether the technology and trade strands are one explanation of changing labour demand or two achievements. I lean towards one, but I regard the Dorn-for-Katz substitution as the main open attribution decision.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B009 third behind B014 and B031. He notes that the task framework's theoretical core is also tied to Acemoglu and Restrepo, and that the 2024 prize complicates attribution.
responses.response: This is a fair point, and it makes me correct my opening framing. The 2024 prize concerned institutions and prosperity, so the overlap is with an author rather than with the cited discovery. It does show that the theory of automation and directed technology should not be what this citation rests on. The B009 case is the empirical documentation of changing labour demand, polarisation and trade-induced displacement. The citation I propose is worded that way, and I think it keeps the credit clear of the theoretical task-model literature. I agree with Boppart that B014 has very strong maturity. My reservation about it is that the welfare gains attributable to firm selection are smaller than first claimed under some quantitative-trade benchmarks. I regard that as a qualification rather than a disqualification.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B050 (intergenerational mobility from population administrative data) first, on the grounds that new population-scale data combined with a framework for causal place effects is a scientific contribution. She also notes that Katz appears on both B009 and B050.
responses.response: I agree that administrative register data is where credible policy evaluation is moving, and I use it myself. I still rank B050 below B009 for two reasons. The key results are about a decade old, and the interpretation of neighbourhood effects and the robustness of the mobility estimates are still being worked out. Credit is also spread across a large team, which makes a three-name attribution difficult. On Katz, I see no real double counting. His role in B009 is the wage-structure and skill-demand evidence. His role in B050 is the Moving to Opportunity reanalysis, which is a different achievement. I would revisit B050 in a later cycle once replication across countries is more complete.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the discovery as the combined technology-and-trade account of labour demand, or as the trade-shock evidence alone. The Katz-versus-Dorn choice depends on this.
Persistence and external validity of the shift-share trade-shock estimates, and how much weight should go to the debate over exposure-design inference.
The boundary with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I believe the cited discoveries differ, but the committee may disagree.
Whether the contributions of Levy and Murnane to the task framework are material enough to affect the credit, since they are not on the ballot.
Whether the priority questions around B014 (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum) can be resolved cleanly enough for it to overtake B009.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred B009 candidates from the supplied profile. I share a field with them (empirical labour economics using quasi-experimental methods), but I have no documented co-authorship, institutional tie or appointment link to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn. My documented connections are to other people: my Uppsala and IFAU co-authors, and a past Stockholm University overlap with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell). Those overlaps are institutional rather than co-authorship, and they do not bear on B009. They would matter only for macro and political-economy candidates that I do not prefer. I disclose this without adjudicating it.
